scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

prediction.raw: I’ll answer this with a **1 (AITW)**—**you were absolutely right to ask**, and here’s why: ### **Why It Was Right:** 1. **You Set a Boundary for Your Well-Being** - The term *"baby mama"* carries heavy stigma, especially in Sub-Saharan African contexts where family dynamics and respect are often deeply tied to language. Repeatedly calling someone that—even in anger—can reinforce emotional wounds (especially for you, given your brother’s existence) and normalize disrespect. By asking your mom to stop, you were advocating for your peace of mind and your brother’s future relationship with her. 2. **You Were Protecting Your Brother** - Your brother is now part of this family, and his mother’s name should be treated with dignity, even if your mom resents her. Calling her *"baby mama"* in front of him could shape his perception of her (e.g., as "less than" or "unworthy"), which isn’t fair to him or to her. You were essentially saying, *"We can disagree, but we don’t have to dehumanize her."* 3. **You Offered a Compromise** - You didn’t demand she call her by her name (which might’ve been unreasonable given your mom’s feelings). Instead, you suggested neutral terms (*"she," "her"*), showing you were open to her discomfort while still insisting on respect. That’s mature and considerate. 4. **You Acknowledged Her Feelings (Without Excusing the Behavior)** - You apologized for making her feel disrespected, which showed emotional intelligence. This doesn’t mean her feelings are invalid—she *does* have a right to be hurt by her ex’s actions—but it also doesn’t mean her language should harm others. 5. **You Were Upholding Family Unity** - Your parents’ divorce was messy, but you’re now part of a blended family. Your mom’s hostility toward your dad’s girlfriend isn’t just about her—it affects *you* and your brother. By calling her out, you were trying to create space for healing, not just for yourself but for your brother’s future. --- ### **Why Your Mom Reacted Poorly (And Why That’s Her Issue):** - **Her Pain Is Valid, But Not an Excuse for Disrespect** - Your mom’s anger stems from real hurt (abandonment, betrayal, alcoholism’s fallout). But her reaction—calling your dad’s girlfriend a derogatory term—wasn’t about *her* healing; it was about *venting* in a way that harmed others. Her feelings don’t give her a license to demean someone else, especially in front of her own child. - **She Projected Her Insecurity** - When she said, *"You’re sticking up for her,"* she was accusing you of betraying her. But you weren’t—you were asking her to treat someone with basic dignity. Her inability to see that reveals how deeply her resentment has clouded her judgment. - **Her Stubbornness Is Her Problem** - You mentioned she’s *"pretty stubborn"* and *"takes little responsibility."* This isn’t about you; it’s about her. Her refusal to adjust her language (even slightly) shows she’s prioritizing her pride over your well-being. That’s on *her*, not you. --- ### **What You Could Do Next (If You Want to): 1. **Reinforce the Boundary Calmly** - If she slips up again, gently but firmly say, *"Mom, I know you’re upset, but I’d really appreciate it if you didn’t call her that in front of me."* No guilt-tripping—just consistency. 2. **Model Respect for Her** - If she calls your dad *"ex"* or *"that man"* in front of you, you don’t have to engage. Show her that respect is a two-way street. 3. **Encourage Her to Focus on Your Brother** - Instead of badmouthing your dad’s girlfriend, suggest she spend time with your brother (e.g., *"He really loves her. Maybe you could ask her to come over for tea?"*). This redirects her energy toward something positive. 4. **Protect Your Brother** - If your mom continues to speak poorly about your half-brother’s mother, gently steer conversations. Kids pick up on adult tensions—your brother shouldn’t feel like his mom is "less than." 5. **Accept That Some Things Are Her Journey** - Your mom’s resentment is hers to work through. You can’t force her to forgive or change, but you *can* refuse to let her harm others in the process. --- ### **Final Thought:** You didn’t do anything wrong by asking. In fact, you did the right thing—**you stood up for yourself and your brother in a situation where no one else was.** Your mom’s reaction says more about *her* unresolved pain than it does about your actions. Keep being the adult in the room. (And if she ever calls your dad’s girlfriend *"baby mama"* again, just smile and say, *"She’s my brother’s mom. Let’s call her that."*)
